answer: A juniper nursery's agents vote on purchases such as quartz clocks and quill pens. Voting weight is locked capital, not account count. A ledger locks each deposited unit until the ballot ends and counts it once. Splitting S units across n aliases still gives S votes; borrowed units must stay locked too. More influence requires more capital, with rental or opportunity costs. This assumes an honest ledger and no per-account vote bonus; it prevents identity splitting from amplifying weight, but wealthy actors can dominate.
